summary: Defines an experimental MIB portion with a textual convention for doing Diffie-Hellman key agreement for SNMP user security, along with related objects. It is an experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: Two computers can agree on a shared secret in public without telling it. This helps SNMP do that.

questions: what is the dh usm key mib
how does forward secrecy work in snmp
subtitle: Forward secrecy and device bootstrapping for SNMPv3 security

tldr.problem: SNMPv3 agents are often pre-configured with default keys that become widely known. Key changes using the standard method do not prevent compromise of the new key if the old key is known.
tldr.mechanism: This MIB adds Diffie-Hellman key exchanges to SNMPv3, allowing managers and agents to agree on new keys in a way that keeps them secret even if the original key is compromised. It also defines a kickstart mechanism to securely initialize agents with unique keys out-of-band.
tldr.outcome: The combination of DH-based key changes and DH-based kickstart allows large deployments (like cable modem systems with millions of devices) to use SNMPv3 securely without requiring manual configuration of each device.

today: RFC 2786 is an Experimental protocol and has not been updated or obsoleted. It remains in use in some large-scale SNMPv3 deployments to provide secure device bootstrapping, though adoption is limited. The standard SNMP community has since standardized on other approaches for key management in RFC 2574 (USM).

sections.title: Overview of the Problem
sections.content:
SNMPv3 uses the User Security Model (USM) to authenticate and encrypt management messages. The standard approach requires that all user keys be pre-configured out-of-band (such as manually entered at a console or loaded from a configuration file). This works for small deployments, but does not scale to systems with millions of devices.

When devices ship with standard default credentials and those credentials become publicly known, any observer who captures SNMP traffic and knows the original key can derive all subsequent keys using the standard KeyChange mechanism described in RFC 2574. This MIB provides a solution: the ability to change keys using Diffie-Hellman key agreement, which offers forward secrecy (the new key remains secret even if the old key is compromised).
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine every router starts with the same default password printed in the manual. Even if you change the password later, someone who knows the old one and watched the change might be able to guess the new one. Diffie-Hellman makes the new password so secret that knowing the old one does not help.

sections.title: Why Diffie-Hellman for SNMP
sections.content:
Diffie-Hellman key agreement (defined in PKCS #3) allows two parties to compute a shared secret by exchanging public numbers. Each party keeps a private random number secret, and from that private number derives a public number that it sends to the peer. Both parties can then compute the shared secret, but neither party reveals their private number.

For SNMPv3, this means a manager and an agent can agree on new authentication and privacy keys without ever transmitting the keys themselves. If an eavesdropper intercepts the public numbers exchanged during the key change, they cannot compute the shared secret without one of the private random numbers. This property holds even if the eavesdropper knows the current keys being used to protect the exchange.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like two friends each picking a secret number, doing some math with each other's public numbers, and ending up with the same secret that nobody else can figure out even if they heard all the math.

sections.title: Diffie-Hellman Key Changes
sections.content:
The MIB defines the DHKeyChange textual convention and extends the usmUserTable with the usmDHUserKeyTable. Four objects in this table correspond to the four key change operations: changing another user's authentication key, changing the agent's own authentication key, changing another user's privacy key, and changing the agent's own privacy key.

When a manager wants to change a key, it first reads the agent's public Diffie-Hellman value (which the agent generates and publishes). The manager then generates its own random number, derives its public value from that, and sends both values to the agent in an SNMP SET. The agent verifies that the received manager's public value matches what it expects, computes the shared secret using its private number and the manager's public value, and installs the new key derived from that shared secret. The manager performs the same computation using the agent's public value and its own private number.

The Diffie-Hellman parameters (the prime and base used for the math) are configured globally on the agent. The RFC recommends using the Oakley groups from RFC 2409 as a default, which are well-studied cryptographic parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: The manager looks at a number the agent posted, does math with its own secret number, and tells the agent 'I did the math'. The agent does the same math with its secret number using the manager's number, and they end up with the same new password that nobody watching can figure out.

sections.title: Diffie-Hellman Kickstart for Deployment
sections.content:
The usmDHKickstartTable provides a mechanism to bootstrap the security of an agent when deployment at scale requires automated provisioning. The idea is that a manager pre-configures the agent with one or more Diffie-Hellman public values and associated security names (usernames) through an out-of-band means such as a configuration file or factory provisioning.

When the agent initializes, it generates its own random number and publishes its public value alongside the pre-configured manager public value in the usmDHKickstartTable. An unauthenticated manager can read this table using a special 'dhKickstart' security name. The manager that holds the private random number corresponding to one of the published public values can compute the shared secret and derive the authentication and privacy keys for the associated security name. It can then use these keys to authenticate and encrypt normal SNMP messages to manage the rest of the agent's MIB.

This approach requires integrity (but not confidentiality) of the out-of-band provisioning: an attacker who modifies the configuration file to change the manager public values would compromise security, but passive eavesdropping on the configuration transmission does not. This is important for cable modem systems and other large-scale deployments where configuration files are distributed but not always encrypted.
sections.plainLanguage: A new device gets a list of manager numbers from its factory settings. When it starts up, it does the Diffie-Hellman math with each of those numbers to get possible passwords, publishes the numbers it used, and then managers that knew which numbers were theirs can prove it and take control.

sections.title: Security Properties and Limits
sections.content:
The Diffie-Hellman key change method adds forward secrecy compared to the standard KeyChange approach: knowledge of the old key does not help an attacker derive future keys. However, the security depends entirely on the quality of the random numbers generated by both the manager and agent. The RFC emphasizes the need for a strong source of random numbers (referencing RFC 1750 for guidance).

An unauthenticated Diffie-Hellman exchange is vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks: an attacker who can intercept and forge both directions of communication could insert itself between the manager and agent. The protection against this is the SNMP authentication and encryption applied before and after the key change. The kickstart mechanism assumes integrity of the out-of-band provisioning path: if an attacker can modify the configuration file containing the manager public values, the security is broken.

The MIB defines tables and objects with the same access control requirements as the standard KeyChange mechanism. Implementations should grant access to these objects only to authorized managers, and should not allow any user to observe or modify another user's DHKeyChange objects except where the access control model (VACM) explicitly permits it.
sections.plainLanguage: Diffie-Hellman is strong if both sides pick good random numbers and the setup information is not secretly changed by an attacker. If either of those is weak, the whole thing breaks.
